# The Last Watch of the Mara Celeste

## I.

The first letter came from a company called Archipelago Maritime Holdings, which I know because I was the one who carried it up from the mail drop in Hamilton. The envelope was cream-colored and heavy, the kind that costs more than the paper inside it warrants, and it was addressed to Captain Wen Li-Fen, care of the *Mara Celeste*, Berth 19, Hamilton Harbor, Bermuda. Captain Wen opened that one. She read it at the galley table while I was peeling ginger for the soup, and when she set it down her face had not changed but her hand went to the edge of the table and stayed there, pressing, as if she were checking that the wood was still solid.

I should say what the *Mara Celeste* was.

She was a forty-six-foot wooden trawler, built in 1951 at a yard in Keelung that no longer exists. Wen's grandfather, Li Dao-Ming, commissioned her for the mackerel runs between Taiwan and the Ryukyus. She had a clinker-built hull of camphor wood and Formosan cypress, which gives off a particular smell when it gets wet—something between temple incense and wet leaves, a smell I have never encountered anywhere else and do not expect to again. Her wheelhouse was small, barely room for two, and the wheel itself was original: a six-spoke wheel of Java teak that had gone dark as coffee from decades of oil and grip. If you ran your hand along the upper spoke at the ten-o'clock position, you could feel the groove where Li Dao-Ming's thumb had pressed during all those years of Pacific crossings. His son—Wen's father, Li Jun-Wei—deepened the groove. And Wen deepened it further, though by the time I served aboard, the groove was less a mark of any single hand and more like the wear on a church step: evidence of repetition so sustained it becomes geology.

She was not a beautiful boat. I want to be clear about that. Her paint was always peeling somewhere. The bilge pump was temperamental and had to be coaxed, spoken to, occasionally struck with the heel of a palm in a specific spot that Wen showed me my first week aboard. The galley was so narrow that I could stand in the middle and touch both walls, which I sometimes did during rough weather to steady myself while the pot slid on the gimbaled stove. She listed faintly to starboard in calm seas, a lean so slight you might not notice it until you set a glass down on the galley table and watched it drift, very slowly, toward the wall where I had pinned a calendar from the fishmonger in St. George's.

The *Mara Celeste* smelled of camphor and diesel and fish that no amount of scrubbing could remove from the hold, a smell that had migrated into the wood the way tea stains the inside of a cup. She was, by any objective measure, a working vessel past her prime, held together by epoxy and stubbornness and the fact that Wen could fix nearly anything aboard with her own hands. She had her grandfather's toolbox. The wrenches still had his grip tape on them, dried almost to powder.

I know the names on the letters because I stopped throwing them away after the third month, when it became clear that the captain was not going to open them. There are things a cook is not supposed to do aboard a vessel, and reading the captain's mail is certainly one of them, but I read them because no one else was going to and because I had come to understand, by then, that someone should know the specific dimensions of what was coming. Archipelago Maritime Holdings had purchased the *Mara Celeste*'s debt from the original lender after Li Jun-Wei died. The boat was collateral. Three years of loan payments had not been made—the first two by Wen's father, who was ill and then dead, and the last by Wen, who was not ill but who was trying to fish the Atlantic mackerel run with a seventy-year-old trawler and a crew of three and who was, if I am being honest, not catching enough fish. The seizure order was filed in a court in Hamilton. The repo men—two of them, I gathered, though maybe it was one man and a lawyer—had reserved Berth 7 in Hamilton Harbor and were scheduled to take possession of the *Mara Celeste* on the eleventh of September.

We were four hundred nautical miles southeast of Bermuda when the eleventh of September came and went, heading not toward Hamilton but into the path of Typhoon Elara, which the maritime weather service had been broadcasting about for two days and which Wen had plotted on the chart with the same small, precise pencil marks she used for everything. She did not discuss the decision with me. She did not discuss the decision with Pau, the deckhand, or with Mal, who handled the nets. She changed course on the ninth, sometime during my sleep shift, and when I came up to the galley at four in the morning to start the rice, the barometer had already dropped eight millibars and the swell had changed character—longer, more deliberate, the kind of swell that is a message from something still over the horizon.

I knew what she had chosen. I cannot tell you the precise moment I knew, whether it was the course change or the letters or something earlier and less specific—a shift in the way she sat at meals, perhaps, or the night I found her in the wheelhouse at two in the morning with her hand in the groove on the wheel, just resting it there, the way you might rest your hand on a sleeping dog. But I knew. And I think she knew I knew, because she looked at me that morning over the chart table and said nothing, and her saying nothing in that particular way was the most honest conversation we ever had.

The men from Archipelago Maritime Holdings waited at Berth 7 for three days, according to the harbor report I obtained later. Then they filed additional paperwork and went home. They had come to collect a boat, and the boat was not there, because the boat was with its captain in the open Atlantic, heading east into the only thing that could not file a lien against it.

---

## II.

I make tea a certain way. I have always made it a certain way, and this is not incidental to anything.

The kettle aboard the *Mara Celeste* was aluminum, dented on its left side from the time it fell during the nor'easter off Cape Hatteras, and it fit on the gimbaled stove as if it had been cast for it, which in a sense it had—the gimbal ring had been bent, over years, to accommodate the kettle's specific shape, and the kettle's base had been worn, over years, to fit the gimbal ring, so that the two objects had become a single system, the way old married couples develop a shared gait. The water aboard was stored in a tank beneath the galley deck and had a mineral taste that changed depending on where we had last filled it. In Hamilton the water tasted of limestone. In St. George's it tasted of nothing. On this trip, the last fill had been Hamilton, so the tea had a faint chalky undertone that I compensated for with an extra few seconds of steeping.

Captain Wen drank oolong. Not any particular oolong; she was not fussy that way. But it had to be loose-leaf, because her grandfather had drunk loose-leaf, and it had to be brewed in a particular small pot—a brown clay pot, Yixing ware, that had no lid anymore because the lid had been broken by Li Jun-Wei during a storm in 1987 and never replaced. Wen brewed it open, which is wrong, but she said the pot knew what to do by now, and I think she may have been right, because the tea that pot produced was better than it had any right to be given the water and the leaves and the absent lid.

I brought the first cup to the wheelhouse at six in the morning on the first full day of the storm. The barometer read 996 millibars, and through the wheelhouse glass the sea had turned the color of wet slate. The swells were perhaps four meters and building, still organized, still with discernible peaks and troughs, but the wind had a constancy to it that I could feel in the vibration of the cup against the saucer as I carried it up the four steps from the galley. I had wedged a folded cloth between the cup and the saucer to prevent it from sliding, which was a technique I had developed during the Hatteras storm and which I was vaguely proud of though I had never mentioned it to anyone.

Wen was at the wheel. She was wearing the canvas jacket she always wore, the one with the mended left pocket whose lining I had re-stitched twice, and her hands were at ten and two, her thumb in the groove. She nodded when I set the tea on the ledge beside the barometer. The ledge was a shelf that Li Dao-Ming had built for the express purpose of holding a teacup, which tells you something about the priorities of the man who designed this vessel.

I went back down to the galley and began preparing the morning rice. The pot had to be double-secured in the gimbal now; I used the wire clamp that lived in the third drawer. The rice took forty minutes. When it was done, I portioned it into two bowls and carried Wen's up to the wheelhouse. The tea was untouched. The surface of it had a slight tremor—a continuous, fine vibration from the hull's interaction with the swell. It had gone cold. I could tell without touching it because the color had changed the way oolong does when it cools: darker, flatter, the surface losing that faint oily sheen that fresh-brewed tea carries.

I picked up the cup, carried it down, poured it into the sink, rinsed the cup with hot water from the kettle, and brewed a fresh pot. I brought the new cup up at a quarter past seven. Wen had not changed position. The rice bowl sat beside the barometer where the tea had been. It was also untouched, but the chopsticks had been moved, which meant Wen had picked them up and then set them down again, and this small evidence of aborted intention was, for a reason I did not examine and do not intend to examine now, the detail that made my throat constrict.

I set the fresh tea beside the rice. I went below.

At half past eight I returned. The barometer read 991. The ledge was at a faint angle now—not enough to spill water from a full cup, but enough that the tea had settled asymmetrically, a meniscus climbing the cup's left wall. The cup was full and cold. The rice was untouched. Through the glass, the swells had lost their organization; they were confused, colliding with each other from multiple directions, which I knew from experience meant the wind had shifted and the storm was rewriting the sea's geometry. Wen's shoulders had changed. They were higher, set closer to her ears, and her forearms had cords standing out that I could see below the rolled cuffs of her jacket.

I took the cup. I took the rice. I went down. I heated the rice in the pot with a little water to loosen it, and I brewed a third cup of tea, and I brought both up to the wheelhouse. I set them on the ledge. I went below.

I returned at ten and the tea was cold and the rice was cold and the barometer read 987 and the ledge was at an angle steep enough that I had to brace the cup against the barometer housing to keep it from sliding. There was water on the wheelhouse floor—not a lot, just a sheen, from spray that had found its way through the seams around the window frame. Wen's boots were dark with it. The window showed nothing I want to describe yet.

I took the cup and went down and brewed a fourth cup and brought it up and set it on the ledge and went down.

At noon I found the cup on the floor. It had slid off the ledge, which was now at an angle that could no longer be called faint. The cup had not broken—it was a heavy stoneware cup, the kind made to survive vessels and weather—but the tea had spilled across the wheelhouse floor and mixed with the spray water in a pale brown wash. I picked up the cup. I looked at Wen. She was looking straight ahead through the glass at what the sea had become, and her thumb was in the groove, and she did not look at me.

I went down and boiled the kettle and brewed the tea and brought it up and set it on the ledge, pressed firmly between the barometer housing and the frame of the wheelhouse window, and I stayed for a moment, adjusting the cup's position with both hands, making sure it was secure. Wen said, very quietly, "Thank you, Aia." It was the only thing she said to me that entire day.

I went down.

I went up at two and the cup was still there. The tea was cold. I took it down and brewed another cup and brought it up. I went up at four. Cold. I took it down. I brewed another. I carried it up the four steps, which were wet now and required a grip on the rail with my free hand. I set the cup on the ledge. I went down.

This is what I did on the first day of the storm. I am aware of how it sounds. I am aware that a reasonable person might ask why I continued to bring tea to a woman who was not drinking it, aboard a boat that was sailing into a typhoon by choice, in a wheelhouse that was taking water through its seams. I can only tell you that the kettle fit the gimbal and the gimbal held the kettle and the pot knew how to brew without its lid, and these were the facts available to me, and I acted on them.

I do not drink tea anymore. I have not drunk it since. This is not something I decided; it is something that happened to me, the way a scar happens, and when people offer me tea I say no thank you and I do not explain why, because the explanation is not that tea reminds me of the *Mara Celeste*. The explanation is that tea *is* the *Mara Celeste*. It is the cup on the ledge and the trembling surface and Wen's shoulders rising and the barometer dropping eight, thirteen, twenty millibars across a single day, and it is my hands adjusting the cup's position to keep it from falling, and it is the sound of the word *Aia* spoken very quietly in a wheelhouse that smelled of salt and camphor and cold oolong.

Every morning since, I make two cups. I pour one out.

---

## III.

We had been playing *cài pái* since I came aboard, which was fourteen months before the storm and three months before the first Archipelago letter. *Cài pái* is not a sophisticated game. It is a two-player game for people who are stuck together on a small boat and need something to do with their hands during the hours between tasks, and it requires more stubbornness than skill, which suited us both.

The deck was older than either of us. It was a set of cards Wen's father had bought at a night market in Kaohsiung sometime in the 1970s—you could tell by the printing, which had that particular muddy registration that cheap Taiwanese color printing had before the industry modernized. The queens had a magenta bleed around their outlines. The backs showed a pattern of blue fish that might have been tuna or might have been bonito; it was impossible to tell anymore because the ink had worn to a kind of general blue suggestion on most of the cards. The seven of diamonds was missing. We used a piece of card stock I had cut from a cereal box, with "7♦" written on it in ballpoint pen, and we both knew it by feel—it was slightly thicker than the other cards, and slightly stiffer, and Wen always accused me of knowing when she was holding it and adjusting my play, which I deny, although she was not entirely wrong.

The tally was kept in a small notebook, the kind with a mottled black-and-white cover that schoolchildren use. It lived in the galley's second drawer, beneath the wire clamp for the rice pot. We had been keeping it since my second week aboard, when Wen won eleven hands in a row and I said something about wanting a record so that when my luck turned I would have proof of the deficit I had overcome, and Wen said that was the most optimistic thing she had ever heard anyone say, and she got the notebook, and she wrote the date and the score at the top of the first page in her small, square handwriting.

Fourteen months of scores. The pages were stained with things I could identify—soy sauce, tea, fish oil from my hands—and things I could not.
